analysis.one_liner: Requires human oversight, bias testing, and appeal rights when employers use AI to make workplace decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 3, 2025 with 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats and 1 Republican) and referred to three House committees; none has taken it up and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set rules for employers that use automated decision systems — software and AI that score, rank, screen, or manage workers. Employers could no longer let such a system be the only decision-maker in hiring, firing, discipline, pay, or scheduling. Before using the software, they would have to test it for accuracy and discrimination, run an independent bias audit every year and publish the results, tell workers in plain language how the system works and what data it uses, have a qualified human confirm the output, give workers the documentation behind any decision within 7 days, and let them dispute it and appeal to a human. Workers could also opt out of being managed by software and get a human manager instead. The bill creates a new Technology and Worker Protection Division in the Labor Department to write rules and enforce them, protects workers who complain from retaliation, lets workers and unions sue with statutory damages of $5,000 to $20,000 per violation, lets state attorneys general sue, and bars employers from forcing these disputes into arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more employees, including federal, congressional, state, and tribal government workers. They gain the right to know when software is being used to judge them, get a plain-language explanation and the input data behind any decision within 7 days at no cost, dispute and appeal the decision to a qualified human, opt out of algorithmic management and get a human supervisor, and be protected from retaliation for complaining. Workers and their unions could sue in court with statutory damages, attorney's fees, and no forced arbitration. Workers covered by anti-discrimination law gain an extra layer of protection, since every system would have to be tested for discriminatory impact based on race, sex, age, disability, pregnancy, and other protected traits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers screened or managed by AI

how_it_helps.text: Bans relying exclusively on an automated decision system for any hiring, firing, discipline, pay, scheduling, or promotion decision, and requires meaningful human oversight of any system output before it is used [S2].

Requires pre-deployment testing of each system for efficacy and compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws, plus independent annual audits for discriminatory impact whose results must be made public [S2].

Requires employers to disclose in plain language what the system does, what data it collects, and how to dispute it, and to give workers full documentation of any decision within 7 days at no cost, with a right to dispute and appeal to a human [S2].
Gives workers managed by an automated system the right to opt out and be managed by a human who can make employment decisions [S2].

Protects workers from retaliation for exercising these rights, and gives workers and unions a private right of action with statutory damages from $5,000 to $20,000 per violation (up to $40,000 for willful or repeated violations), attorney's fees, and invalidation of predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims [S2].
Covers federal, congressional, state, and tribal government employees, waiving sovereign immunity for state and tribal programs that receive federal financial assistance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers — including staffing intermediaries, public agencies, and Congress's own employing offices — bear the cost of testing and validating each system, annual independent bias audits, drafting plain-language disclosures, training staff who operate the systems, producing documentation of decisions within 7 days, and staffing human reviewers and appeal channels. They also face exposure to statutory damages lawsuits and lose the ability to force workers into arbitration over these claims. Vendors of workplace AI face liability and disclosure demands that could require redesigning products.

drawbacks.text: The definition of an automated decision system is very broad — it covers any software that aids decisions using computation, including statistics — so even small employers just over the 11-employee threshold could face testing, audit, disclosure, and documentation duties for ordinary HR software [S2].

The bill's statutory damages ($5,000 to $20,000 per violation, treble damages available) and attorney's-fee awards, combined with a broad private right of action and invalidation of arbitration clauses, could generate substantial litigation against employers [S2].

Annual independent audits and pre-deployment validation of every covered system are recurring costs, and employers using many systems across hiring, scheduling, and monitoring would bear them for each one [S2].

Employers lose flexibility: they can no longer rely on a system alone for any employment decision and must employ or designate humans with relevant experience to corroborate outputs and hear appeals, which is a real operational cost for high-volume employers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: workers get transparency, a human backstop, and a way to fight an algorithmic firing or bad scheduling score, at the price of meaningful compliance costs for employers and litigation exposure. The protections are targeted at a genuine, growing problem — software that screens resumes, monitors productivity, and assigns shifts with little recourse — and the human-oversight and appeal requirements are the heart of the bill, not window dressing. The main design weaknesses are the breadth of the covered-system definition relative to the low 11-employee coverage threshold, which sweeps in small employers using ordinary software, and a damages scheme that could invite lawsuits over paperwork violations rather than harmful decisions.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in early December 2025 and sent to three House committees — Education and Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform — and none has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Representative Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on December 3, 2025, joined by Representatives Chris Deluzio and James Moylan as original cosponsors [S2][S4].
The House referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee as the primary committee, and in addition to the House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform Committees [S4][S1].
The bill has 13 cosponsors: 12 of 217 House Democrats and 1 of 223 House Republicans [S3].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action — appears in the bill's action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the bill, which leaves employers using workplace AI and the vendors that sell it operating under the current rules, with no new testing, disclosure, or appeal obligations. Workers keep the status quo, including opaque algorithmic decisions with no federal right to a human review.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and AI HR vendors, for now

sides.party_line_note: Thirteen of the fourteen supporters are Democrats; the only Republican is Guam's non-voting delegate, no Republican has opposed it on the record, and no votes have occurred yet.

industries.industry: Workplace AI and HR software vendors
industries.note: Firms selling hiring, monitoring, scheduling, and productivity-scoring systems would have to pass pre-deployment testing and annual independent bias audits, disclose their systems' inputs and workings, and give up sole decision authority. Their interest in keeping products opaque and unaudited runs against the worker protections the bill creates.

Employers bear testing, audit, disclosure, training, documentation, and human-review costs, plus statutory-damages litigation exposure, and lose forced arbitration for these claims. The savings from automating management decisions without oversight are exactly what the bill targets.

The bill mandates pre-deployment validation and annual independent bias audits with public results, creating a new market for third-party auditors. Their business grows only if the worker protections take effect.

Unions get standing to sue over violations on behalf of members, seats on the new Labor Department advisory boards, and an exemption from the employer definition. Their gains track the gains the bill gives workers.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term labor bill with 14 supporters, referred to three committees in December of the first session under a Republican House majority that has shown no movement on it, will most likely sit without a hearing or markup and die when the Congress ends, unless its provisions are attached to a larger package. Its one Republican cosponsor is a non-voting delegate, so the bill has essentially no path to floor action as introduced.
